transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-01-28
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Alice Bennett (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maria Lopez (Acme CTO), Daniel Kim (Staff Eng), Jin Park (Infra)

---
Summary (auto):
Quick technical deep dive focused on p95/p99 tail latency, streaming vs non-streaming, and network topology. Action items and benchmarking plan agreed.

---
Transcript:
[00:00:00] Alice (Redwood): okay hey everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to make this a focused deep dive on tail latency — p95/p99 and p99.9 — and practical mitigations for Acme's inference traffic.
[00:00:18] Maria (Acme): yep thanks, our customers are sensitive to spikes. Average latency looks fine but p99 is killing us, sometimes pages take 2–3x the normal.
[00:00:30] Samir (Redwood): yeah that's common. First quick note: are you mostly streaming responses to clients or returning full-assembled responses?
[00:00:40] Daniel (Acme): currently non-streaming for the main product; we switched to streaming in a few beta paths but most requests still wait for full generation.
[00:00:52] Jin (Acme): infra-wise we use an ELB in front, then a sidecar that talks to the Redwood endpoint in the VPC peered environment.
[00:01:05] Samir: cool. So there are a couple of categories for tail latency: model compute variance, KV cache cold misses, batching head-of-line blocking, network jitter/hops, and occasional infra GC or node churn. We'll go through each.

[00:01:30] Alice: also, worth noting we saw a few mis-tran scripts where people say KV cash or Key-V cache — just FYI — but it's the same thing.

[00:01:40] Maria: ha, yeah we've seen transcription artifacts too. but real question — what do you recommend first?

[00:01:48] Samir: immediate wins are twofold: reduce network hops and get the KV cache warmed for the active prompt prefixes. For network we want to minimize client-to-GPU hops (eg client -> LB -> infra -> GPU). Co-locate inference closer to the caller where possible, or use a regional pop. For your VPC setup, VPC peering and private link reduce hop count and TLS overhead.

[00:02:15] Daniel: we actually have a cross-region setup for redundancy, so sometimes requests go inter-region. Can that blow up p99?
[00:02:24] Samir: yes, inter-region adds tail risk. If failover is synchronous it can double or triple latency for some requests. We recommend region-aware routing and sticky sessions to reduce cross-region fans.

[00:02:38] Jin: on the KV cache, how do you approach warming? our traffic is bursty and prefixes vary a bit.

[00:02:46] Samir: two patterns: proactive warm (preload common prefixes during deployment or warm pools) and on-demand background warming. Redwood's runtime supports prefix caching — we can pre-warm top-n prefixes from your example prompt set. Also warm pools: keep a small set of model instances hot so KV caches persist across requests.

[00:03:10] Maria: does warm pool cost a lot? CFO will ask.

[00:03:15] Alice: it's a tradeoff — warm pools cost reserved capacity but often pay off vs SLA penalties and user churn. We'll show a cost vs latency curve from our last customer where a 10% commit cut p99 in half.

[00:03:30] Daniel: batching — we've seen odd behavior when we increase batch size; small fraction of requests hang waiting for full batch. head-of-line problem?

[00:03:40] Samir: exactly, head-of-line blocking is when a long request sits at front of batch and holds others. Two mitigations: dynamic batching with deadline-based release (you cap wait time) and size-aware routing so short queries get fast-path lanes. Redwood supports continuous batching that groups by expected token length to reduce variance in batch. Also reserving small fast lanes for <64-token requests helps.

[00:04:12] Jin: what's the trade with quantization? we tried int8 and saw slightly higher latency for some ops.

[00:04:19] Samir: quantization reduces memory and can accelerate int-matmul heavy ops, but sometimes kernel selection makes certain attention kernels slower at small sequence lengths. Also quantization can change cache behavior — value sizes differ and may increase copy overhead. Our docs have per-model recommendations: e.g., Llama2-70B-qlora int8 gives big throughput gains on A100 but watch tail latency at short seq lengths. We'll send the recommendation doc.

[00:04:52] Alice: we should also talk streaming vs non-streaming — perceived latency can be dramatically different. If you stream token deltas, p95 perceived is often much better because users see the first tokens fast. But streaming adds latency overhead per-chunk (more network ops).

[00:05:08] Maria: our web UI expects full responses for post-processing and reranking. Switching to streaming would require frontend changes. Are there hybrid approaches?

[00:05:18] Samir: yes, hybrid: send the first N tokens fast (prefix generation) in streaming mode then continue non-streaming for the rest. Or partial streaming: stream first chunk for perceived latency, buffer for quality and reranking server-side. You can also do token-level partial scoring.

[00:05:35] Daniel: any quant metrics for streaming vs non-streaming on p99?

[00:05:40] Samir: ballpark — for many workloads streaming can cut p95 by 30–60% for first-contentful-paint, but p99 for full-content still depends on model compute. We measured a case where streaming reduced p95 by 50% but p99 for full response only fell 15%. We'll run the same with your prompt set.

[00:06:02] Jin: network hops — can you explain impact of sidecar vs direct call? we have a sidecar for observability.

[00:06:08] Samir: sidecar adds a process hop and often an extra socket. That doubles jitter probability. If sidecar is necessary, make it in-process or use gRPC with keepalive and connection reuse. Also keep pooling at the client side so you don't get frequent TLS handshakes.

[00:06:27] Alice: we sometimes recommend a co-located gateway in the same subnet as the GPU instances to reduce hops. For Redwood Private that often means customer runs our control plane locally or uses a private link.

[00:06:40] Maria: error budgets — how do we tie p99 SLOs to these mitigations?

[00:06:46] Samir: measure in slices. Start by SLOs for first-token latency (streaming) and full-response latency separately. Also instrument by path: network time, queue time, model compute, streaming overhead. That helps find where p99 is happening.

[00:07:05] Daniel: we have traces but not instrumented for KV misses. What would you need?

[00:07:11] Samir: share traces with timing per stage: request arrival, LB handoff, routing, queue start, batch start, model start, token finish. Even approximate timestamps help. Also token distribution histogram (how many requests by expected token length) so we can simulate realistic batching.

[00:07:34] Jin: what about preemption and node heterogeneity? we run mixed instance types.

[00:07:40] Samir: mixed nodes increase tail risk. Preemption, noisy neighbors, or hotspots cause a small fraction of requests to run on slower hardware, inflating p99. Best practice: homogeneous pools for latency-sensitive routes, or label-based routing that pins high-SLO traffic to dedicated pool.

[00:07:58] Maria: you mentioned circuit breakers and fallback models earlier — can you expand?

[00:08:05] Samir: yes — set thresholds on queue wait and model compute. If queue wait exceeds X ms, route to a smaller/fast model variant or return a cached response. For example, degrade from Llama2-70B to a 13B quantized variant as fallback. Also maintain a small fast LRU cache of recent requests for hot queries.

[00:08:25] Alice: we've seen customers reduce p99 spikes by 40% with fallback variants + cache hit rates of 12-18% on repeat prompts.

[00:08:35] Daniel: about benchmarking: what test harness do you recommend?

[00:08:40] Samir: run three tiers: steady-state at your 95th traffic, spike test (2–5x for short windows), and long tail test (sustained plus randomized slow nodes). Compare streaming vs non-streaming, with and without warm pools, and with KV warmup. Capture p50/p95/p99/p99.9, and resource utilization.

[00:09:05] Maria: can Redwood run those for us?

[00:09:09] Alice: yes we'll run them with your sample prompts once you share them and allow a short access window. We'll provide CSVs and a dashboard link.

[00:09:18] Jin: about VPC/on-prem — if we move to Private, would tail latency improve?

[00:09:24] Samir: likely yes if you can co-locate clients and GPUs, reduce public network hops, and avoid cross-tenant noisy neighbors. But Private adds ops overhead; you still need warm pool planning and monitoring. For critical low-p99 you want dedicated pinned pools in Private.

[00:09:40] Maria: are there known kernel-level issues for attention that cause tails?

[00:09:44] Samir: attention patterns and KV cache flushes can cause big spikes. For long-context workloads KV cache size and eviction policy matter. Also some CUDA kernels have variance depending on sequence length; our runtime chooses kernels to minimize this but sometimes quantized kernels are less stable.

[00:10:05] Daniel: any quick config snippets? e.g., batching timeout and warm pool size heuristics?

[00:10:11] Samir: yes — for your traffic distribution (once you share) we'll recommend specific params. Common starting points: batching max_wait_ms=25, max_batch_tokens=4096, fast_lane_threshold=64 tokens, warm_pool_size=3-5 instances per route. That tends to reduce p99 without massive cost.

[00:10:35] Alice: also enable connection reuse and keepalives, and set TLS session resumption. Small improvements but they stack.

[00:10:43] Maria: anything else on monitoring?

[00:10:46] Samir: track bucketed latency histograms, not only averages. Instrument queue_time and model_time as separate metrics. Alert on shifts in p99, not just error rates.

[00:10:58] Jin: we use Prometheus and Grafana, is that compatible?

[00:11:02] Alice: yes Redwood exposes Prom metrics and you can integrate traces. We'll share config.

[00:11:08] (short side convo about log retention and security, mentions SOC2)

[00:11:25] Maria: ok let's recap and next steps.
[00:11:28] Alice: recap — Redwood will run benchmark suite (streaming vs non-streaming, warm pools on/off, quantized vs FP) once Acme shares prompt set and traces. Samir will send quantization docs and config snippets. Acme will map their network topology and share traces. We'll aim for results by 2025-02-04.

[00:11:50] Daniel: any blockers on the Redwood side for VPC peering?

[00:11:54] Alice: we need a peering request and the network CIDR ranges; we'll share the documented steps. Should be straightforward.

[00:12:02] Maria: thanks all. This was helpful.
[00:12:06] Alice: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the deck and the benchmark plan.

[00:12:10] (meeting end)
